name: Dopamine / porn avoidance

lead: This practice covers avoiding pornography, masturbation and other highly stimulating habits. Followers of NoFap and 'dopamine fasting' do it hoping for higher testosterone, focus and confidence, which they say makes a person come across as more attractive and present.

The chain proponents describe is: abstain, reward system 'resets', more drive and willpower, more confidence. Researchers describe the specific hormone and appearance claims as unsupported. Dopamine fasting itself was developed by psychologist Cameron Sepah as a behavioural tool to reduce impulsive behaviours, not to literally lower dopamine.

paras: In looksmaxxing circles abstaining is listed as a free step alongside fitness and skincare. People track streaks in communities such as NoFap, and dopamine fasting versions cut out phones, snacks or other high-stimulation habits for set periods. Users report changes in focus and mood over weeks.

Surveys found members' mental health problems were more plausibly linked to underlying disorders than to abstinence, and some researchers argue prolonged abstinence may worsen distress. Extreme versions such as sensory deprivation are criticised by clinicians. DSM-5-TR does not recognise porn addiction.

angle.text: Followers of NoFap and dopamine fasting abstain hoping to raise drive, focus and confidence, which they say makes a person come across as more attractive. Researchers describe the hormone and appearance claims as unsupported, though dopamine fasting was developed as a behavioural tool.

lead: Dopamine and porn avoidance is a self-improvement practice in which people step back from pornography, masturbation, short-form video, gaming and similar high-stimulation habits for a set period. Practitioners use it as a way to look and present better: the freed-up time and energy goes into the gym, walking, skincare routines and sleep, and followers describe feeling more confident, more focused and more motivated to keep up appearance-related habits [1][2][3].

Two overlapping movements sit under this heading. NoFap is an online community founded in June 2011 by Alexander Rhodes after a Reddit thread, centred on abstaining from pornography and masturbation. Dopamine fasting was developed by California psychologist Cameron Sepah as a cognitive behavioural tool for impulsive behaviours [1][2]. On looksmax.org, members announce short detoxes (for example, ten days without short-form video or masturbation paired with more daily steps and a topical routine) as a way to reset mood and restart training momentum [3].

Researchers and clinicians have commented on both. Wikipedia reports that the most prominent claimed benefits of NoFap lack supporting evidence and that experts describe many of its views as simplistic [1]. Neuroscientists have criticised the idea of a dopamine reset, and Sepah says the goal is reducing impulsive behaviours rather than lowering dopamine itself [2]. Some forum authors make the same distinction, describing their own detox plans as reducing artificial highs rather than removing dopamine [4].
infobox: Porn addiction not recognised in DSM-5-TR; ICD-11 lists compulsive sexual behaviour disorder as an impulse-control disorder [7]

paras: Versions range from narrow to broad. The narrowest is avoiding pornography, and often masturbation and orgasm, a bundle NoFap members abbreviate as 'PMO' [1]. The broadest adds social media, gaming, junk food, music and notifications, and in its most extreme theoretical form amounts to sensory deprivation [2]. Dopamine fasting itself has no fixed definition: some proponents limit it to online technology, others extend it to work, exercise, physical contact and unnecessary conversation [2].

One widely shared looksmax.org guide stresses that a detox is not about cutting out dopamine but about reducing artificial highs. It suggests lighter measures such as capping social media, keeping the phone out of the bedroom and avoiding screens in the first hour of the morning, replaced by exercise, reading and time outdoors [4]. Others pair a short detox with fitness targets, such as higher daily step counts and a set weekly routine for a skincare or hair device [3].

The looks angle runs through behaviour. Time and attention previously spent scrolling are redirected to training, sleep and grooming, which are the habits that change physique, skin and presentation. A related page covers the sleep-focused version, in which screens are switched off before bed.

NoFap began in June 2011 when Pittsburgh web developer Alexander Rhodes read a Reddit thread about a 2003 study that claimed testosterone rose sharply on the seventh day of abstinence; the thread reached Reddit's front page, and the NoFap subreddit launched on 20 June 2011 [1]. The 2003 paper was retracted in 2021 after it was found to overlap with a Chinese-language publication [1]. Rhodes has said the word came from bodybuilding slang and was initially a joke [1].

Membership more than tripled in about two years, prompting Rhodes to build a separate forum at NoFap.com, and in April 2015 he reportedly left a job at Google to work on it full time [1]. Registered forum membership passed 350,000 by January 2024, and the site's infobox gave about 1.2 million users as of August 2025 [1]. Members call themselves 'Fapstronauts' and women participants 'Femstronauts'; a 2014 internet survey found about 99 percent of followers were male, though the figure comes from a source Wikipedia flags as potentially unreliable, and Rhodes estimated about 5 percent were women [1].

Participants range from atheists, Rhodes among them, to fundamentalist Christians [1]. The movement's science draws largely on the writings of anti-pornography activist Gary Wilson, whose lack of medical training has been noted by critics [1]. Members describe benefits such as energy, focus and sleep, sometimes called 'superpowers' [1].

Dopamine fasting originated with Cameron Sepah, a California psychologist who framed it as a cognitive behavioural technique for impulsive behaviours and coined the name; he has since said the name is misleading [2]. It became widely known in late 2019: Vice ran a piece on 17 October, The New York Times technology reporter Nellie Bowles wrote about it on 7 November, and Psych Central, Mic and Marie Claire followed [2]. Commentators tied it to Silicon Valley biohackers and to a backlash against products designed to hold attention, and proponents present it as a way to encourage reading, crafting and outdoor activity [2].

Wikipedia lists later responses including a UConn Q&A with neuroscientist John Salamone, who described the practice as nebulously defined (January 2020), a Harvard Health blog post by physician Peter Grinspoon (February 2020), and a 2024 Inc. article reporting his view that most dopamine detoxes do more harm than good [2].

Both practices were absorbed into looksmaxxing under terms such as 'motivationmaxxing' and detox challenges. A looksmax.org member quoted in one thread described cutting short-form content, abstaining and raising his step count to improve a flat mood at the gym [3], while another thread proposed a seven-day plan limiting social media to 30 to 60 minutes a day, keeping phones out of the bedroom and replacing screen time with lifting, reading and sunlight [4]. Other long threads cover dopamine receptor pharmacology and supplements marketed for dopamine, outside the abstinence framing [5].

NoFap members cite improved relationships, willpower and mental clarity; goals vary among members, and a 2020 study of Polish internet users noted that the group's official aim is helping people refrain from pornography and reach sexual health goals rather than necessarily ending all masturbation [1]. The commonly advocated target is 90 days [1].

Dopamine fasting proponents say it builds self-discipline. Sepah says the aim is to reduce impulsive behaviours that dopamine rewards, not to lower dopamine; neuroscientist Ciara McCabe describes the practice as avoiding cues, such as a phone's ringtone, that trigger compulsive follow-up behaviour [2]. A New York Times reporter described a practitioner whose daily life became more exciting and fun [2].

In looksmaxxing forums the practice is also bundled with claims about testosterone, confidence and attractiveness, and some threads discuss dopamine receptor pharmacology and supplements aimed at boosting dopamine [5]. Some users also report that a week of cutting out nearly everything left the world feeling flat [6].

A 2020 study by Zimmer and Imhoff in Archives of Sexual Behavior found that motivation to abstain was linked to viewing masturbation as unhealthy, religiosity, conservatism and lower trust in science [1]. A 2018 analysis of NoFap forums by Taylor and Jackson in Sexualities found members rejecting pornography and reproducing traditional ideas of masculinity [1]. A 2021 qualitative study by Chasioti and Binnie found that framing abstinence around relapse appeared to sustain distress [1]. A 2023 preregistered survey by Prause and Binnie in Sexualities reported that members' mental health problems were more plausibly linked to underlying disorders than to abstinence, and the authors described the Reboot/NoFap approach as having harmful effects on public health [1]. A 2020 Social Forces study by Burke and MillerMacPhee found that news coverage of pornography addiction often relied on non-scientists [1].

Psychologist David Ley and therapist Paula Hall say there is little medical evidence for claimed physical benefits, and sociologist Kelsy Burke says there is no scientific evidence for the claimed effects [1].

subs.h: On pornography addiction as a diagnosis
paras: The DSM-5 (2013) and DSM-5-TR (2022) do not recognise porn or sex addiction. ICD-11 (2022) added compulsive sexual behaviour disorder under impulse-control disorders rather than addictive disorders, and the American Society of Addiction Medicine does not list sexual addiction as a diagnosis [1][7]. In 2016 AASECT said there was not enough empirical evidence to classify sex or porn addiction as a mental health disorder [7].

Brain-imaging research is mixed. Kraus et al. (2016) and Gola et al. (2017) reported heightened cue reactivity in the amygdala and ventral striatum among people with compulsive sexual behaviour, similar to drug-cue responses, while Prause and colleagues (2015) reported that key addiction biomarkers were missing [7]. Treatment reviews describe evidence quality as generally low, with some favouring cognitive behavioural therapy and acceptance-based approaches [7]. Critics including Williams, Thomas and Prior (2022) call the concept largely morally and politically motivated, and McKee et al. (2022) argue sexual shame rather than pornography should be the focus [7].

Neuroscience reviews describe dopamine as involved in learning, motivation and movement rather than simply pleasure, which is why researchers say the term 'reset' does not map onto the brain's biology [8]. Peter Grinspoon called Sepah's work sensible if not groundbreaking while criticising followers who adopt ever more ascetic versions, and McCabe disputes the idea that avoiding dopamine triggers resets the brain [2]. Critics argue that removing a stimulus reduces stimulation rather than dopamine, and that literally lowering dopamine would be harmful [2].

Christopher Ferguson (2018) argued that technology use has not been shown to desensitise the brain to dopamine [2]. A 2024 genetically informed study in Computers in Human Behavior of adults aged 30 to 45 found more screen time associated with higher impulsivity, particularly under urgency, though it examined screen time rather than dopamine fasting [2]. Wikipedia also notes that physical activity, which may replace the abandoned habits, is associated with increased grey matter in reward-related brain regions [2].

No controlled clinical trials of porn or dopamine avoidance as a looksmaxxing or appearance intervention were found. Related observational and survey research includes the 2020 survey on motivation to abstain, the 2021 qualitative study of abstinence framed around relapse, and the 2023 preregistered survey of NoFap-style practice by Prause and Binnie [1]. For dopamine fasting, a 2022 paper in Lifestyle Medicine by Fei and colleagues considered it as a possible intervention for behavioural addiction, and the 2024 Computers in Human Behavior study linked screen time to impulsivity [2].

Studies of digital detoxes, a broader category, are mixed: a 2023 meta-analysis found small well-being gains from reduced social media use, a 2024 meta-analysis found reduced depression but no significant effect on well-being or stress, and a month-long randomised trial published in PNAS Nexus in February 2025 found that restricting mobile internet access improved mental health, well-being and sustained attention [9].

Media coverage of NoFap has appeared in outlets including The Telegraph and Business Insider (2013), The Independent (2016, 2017), The Guardian and The New York Times (2019), CNET (2020), Der Spiegel (2021) and NPR (2024), with reporters focusing on the community's links to the manosphere and the lack of scientific support for its claims [1]. Studies of Reddit users found NoFap members were also likely to belong to TheRedPill and pickup-artist communities, and a 2025 study by Perin and Ferrero Camoletto reported members' worry that the group was drifting toward Red Pill and incel ideas [1]. Journalists and researchers have criticised some forum posts as misogynistic, and some posts promoted antisemitic conspiracy theories [1]. Supporters point to members' stories of recovery and discipline.

Wikipedia also reports legal disputes: Rhodes threatened two scientists with litigation, NoFap threatened to sue The Spectator in 2018 over its reporting, and a federal suit filed in the Western District of Pennsylvania by Rhodes against Aylo, UCLA, Taylor & Francis and researchers Nicole Prause and David Ley alleging a conspiracy; Prause has contested the allegations [1].
On looksmax.org, detox threads present screen breaks as a no-cost step alongside training, skincare and sleep, and some posters add supplements or pharmacology aimed at dopamine [3][4][5].

Researchers say prolonged abstinence framed around relapse may sustain distress in some people [1]. Clinicians including Grinspoon caution against extreme dopamine-fasting versions that restrict food, conversation or all stimulation [2]. Forum members who attempt abrupt detoxes sometimes report flat mood or low energy afterward [6]. Critics have linked parts of the NoFap community to misogyny and manosphere ideology, and Rhodes has been involved in litigation against researchers [1].

lore.intro: Abstaining from porn and stimulation is commonly mentioned in looksmaxxing communities as a free step alongside fitness and skincare, with detox threads ranging from short screen breaks to multi-day abstinence challenges [3][4].
